questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A newly qualified nurse is asked to perform an unfamiliar central-line procedure without supervision. What is the most professional response?

options.text: Explain the limitation, seek guidance and arrange supervised practice before proceeding.
Attempt the procedure to avoid appearing inexperienced.
Ask another junior nurse to help.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability includes recognising limits and seeking appropriate preparation and supervision before patient safety is compromised.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes responsibility from accountability?

options.text: Responsibility concerns accepted duties, while accountability means being answerable for decisions and outcomes.
Responsibility ends when a task is delegated.

questions.rationale: The notes distinguish duties accepted within a role from being answerable for decisions and outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse follows a senior clinician's instruction that appears unsafe. Which principle applies?

options.text: The nurse must respectfully question the instruction and escalate if required.
The nurse should act first and document concern later.

questions.rationale: Following an instruction does not remove the nurse's duty to question unsafe care.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which factor most directly defines a nurse's scope of practice?

options.text: The preferences of the shift coordinator.
Law, registration, education, competence and workplace policy.

questions.rationale: Scope is shaped by legal, regulatory, educational, competency and organisational requirements.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A patient offers the nurse an expensive gift after discharge. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline respectfully and explain professional boundaries.
Accept it because the therapeutic relationship has ended.

questions.rationale: Financial or dual relationships may create exploitation, favouritism or loss of objectivity.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates the nurse's advocacy role?

options.text: Speaking up when a patient's expressed preferences are being overlooked.

questions.rationale: Advocacy involves supporting patient rights, preferences and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse is uncertain whether a task is authorised within local policy. What should happen first?

options.text: Proceed if the task seems simple.
Check policy and seek senior guidance before acting.

questions.rationale: Professional practice requires verification of scope and policy before performing unfamiliar or potentially unauthorised work.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse begins sharing personal relationship problems with a patient who offers emotional support. What is the primary concern?

options.text: The patient may become more independent.
The therapeutic relationship is shifting toward a personal dual relationship.

questions.rationale: The relationship exists to meet the patient's needs, not the nurse's personal needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates professional accountability?

options.text: The nurse recognises limits, makes safe decisions, documents care and accepts responsibility for outcomes.
The nurse completes assigned tasks quickly.
The nurse follows every instruction without question.

questions.rationale: Accountability is demonstrated through safe judgement, transparent practice and ownership of decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse notices that a colleague repeatedly performs a procedure without required competency assessment. What is the best action?

options.text: Ignore it because the colleague is experienced.
Raise the concern through the appropriate safety and escalation process.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability includes acting when unsafe practice is observed.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which professional role is demonstrated when a nurse explains a new medicine and checks understanding?
questions.rationale: Education is a core professional nursing role.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse delegates a task and assumes accountability has transferred completely. Why is this incorrect?

options.text: Delegation transfers performance of the task, not the nurse's accountability for appropriate delegation and follow-up.

questions.rationale: The delegating nurse remains accountable for assessing the task, person and outcome.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which action is most likely to damage public trust?

options.text: Hiding an error and altering the record.

questions.rationale: Dishonesty and deceptive documentation undermine patient safety and public trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse receives a social-media request from a current patient. What is the safest response?

options.text: Decline and maintain the professional relationship through approved channels.

questions.rationale: Social-media contact can blur boundaries and create confidentiality risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse feels emotionally overinvolved with one patient. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient about the feelings.
Reflect, seek supervision and restore consistent boundaries.

questions.rationale: Self-awareness and supervision support safe boundaries.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which behaviour best reflects professional identity?

options.text: Consistent knowledge, respectful conduct, sound judgement and responsibility.

questions.rationale: Professional identity is expressed through knowledge, conduct, communication and responsibility.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse is asked to work beyond competence during a staffing shortage. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Explain the concern and seek safe allocation, supervision or support.
Accept because staffing pressure changes scope.
Ask the patient to consent to the risk.

questions.rationale: Workload pressure does not remove professional scope and competence requirements.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which situation is a dual relationship?

options.text: A nurse enters a business partnership with a current patient.
A nurse advocates during discharge planning.
A nurse discusses care in handover.

questions.rationale: Business, financial or personal relationships alongside care can compromise objectivity.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: A professional nurse receives constructive feedback about communication. What is the best response?

options.text: Reject it because no complaint was made.
Reflect on the feedback and identify a practical improvement.

questions.rationale: Professionalism includes reflection and willingness to improve.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Nursing Identity and Accountability
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects professional nursing practice?

options.text: The nurse relies on senior staff for decisions.
The nurse combines competence, accountability, respectful communication and clear boundaries in everyday care.

questions.rationale: Professionalism is shown consistently through everyday behaviour and judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A competent patient refuses a blood transfusion for deeply held beliefs. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Confirm understanding, communicate the refusal and advocate for alternative management.
Pressure the patient to accept because the treatment may save life.
Ask the family to override the decision.

questions.rationale: Autonomy includes the right of a capable person to refuse treatment after receiving adequate information.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which ethical principle is most directly involved when a nurse promotes a patient's wellbeing?
questions.rationale: Beneficence means promoting good.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which principle requires the nurse to avoid or minimise harm?
questions.rationale: Nonmaleficence concerns avoiding or reducing harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A ward has one remaining monitored bed and two patients may benefit. Which principle is most relevant?
questions.rationale: Justice concerns fairness and appropriate distribution of resources.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient, 'The procedure will not hurt,' despite knowing discomfort is likely. Which principle is breached?
questions.rationale: Veracity requires honesty; false reassurance weakens trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates fidelity?

options.text: Giving priority to a preferred patient.
Keeping a professional commitment to return with information.

questions.rationale: Fidelity involves keeping professional promises and commitments.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A treatment offers benefit but also significant burden. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support discussion of benefits, risks, burdens and the patient's preferences.

questions.rationale: Ethical reasoning balances beneficence, nonmaleficence and autonomy.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A patient with capacity chooses an option the team considers unwise. What is the nurse's responsibility?

options.text: Replace the decision with the safest option.
Question the patient's competence because the choice differs from professional advice.
Respect the informed decision while ensuring the patient understands consequences.

questions.rationale: Autonomy includes decisions professionals may not prefer.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which response best preserves dignity?

options.text: Explaining care, providing privacy and involving the patient respectfully.
Discussing intimate care in a public corridor.
Using humour about the patient's condition.

questions.rationale: Dignity requires privacy, respect and participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A nurse notices that patients from one language group receive less detailed education. Which principle is most relevant?
questions.rationale: Unequal access to information raises a fairness and justice concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A patient asks directly about a serious diagnosis that has not yet been discussed by the medical team. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respond honestly within role and arrange appropriate discussion with the responsible clinician.

questions.rationale: Veracity and role clarity require truthful, appropriate communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which action violates autonomy?

options.text: Coercing a capable patient into accepting care.

questions.rationale: Coercion undermines voluntary choice.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Two ethical principles conflict during a complex decision. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Seek structured discussion, senior advice and appropriate ethics support.
Ask the family to resolve it.

questions.rationale: When principles conflict, nurses should seek help and use structured reasoning.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A nurse advocates for equal pain treatment regardless of a patient's background. Which principle is being applied?
questions.rationale: Justice requires fairness and equal respect.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects nonmaleficence?

options.text: Follow patient wishes without discussing harm.
Minimise avoidable harm while recognising that some treatments carry justified risk.
Provide care only when benefit is guaranteed.

questions.rationale: Nonmaleficence requires minimising harm, not eliminating all risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A nurse hides a medication error to protect a colleague. Which ethical duties are breached?
questions.rationale: Hiding the error breaches honesty and professional commitment to safe care.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A patient requests information in plain language. What is the ethical basis for providing it?
questions.rationale: People need understandable information to make autonomous decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A nurse allocates extra time to a very anxious patient while ensuring other patients remain safe. Which ethical reasoning is being used?
questions.rationale: The nurse is balancing individual benefit with fair distribution of care.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates ethical nursing practice?

options.text: The nurse follows policy without considering the patient.
The nurse uses ethical principles to protect dignity, choice, fairness and safety.
The nurse gives identical care in every situation.

questions.rationale: Ethical practice requires thoughtful application of principles to individual care.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Principles and Patient Rights
questions.stem: A patient refuses treatment after receiving understandable information. What should the nurse document?

options.text: Only that the patient was non-compliant.
The nurse's opinion of the decision.
Nothing, because refusal is the patient's right.
The information provided, the patient's understanding and decision, concerns explored and who was informed.

questions.rationale: Clear documentation supports autonomy, continuity and accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which elements are required for valid informed consent?
questions.rationale: Valid consent requires capacity, sufficient information and freedom from coercion.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A patient says they no longer wish to proceed after signing a consent form. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that the signature cannot be withdrawn.
Stop and notify the appropriate clinician because consent may be withdrawn.
Ask the family to persuade the patient.

questions.rationale: Consent is an ongoing process and may be withdrawn.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A relative phones asking for test results, but the nurse cannot verify authority. What is the correct response?

options.text: Ask the caller to identify the diagnosis.
Do not disclose information and follow the authorised communication process.

questions.rationale: Information should be shared only with appropriate authority.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which action is a confidentiality breach?

options.text: Discussing care privately with the treating team.
Talking about a patient's condition in a public lift.

questions.rationale: Public conversations can expose private information.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A nurse writes, 'Patient was rude and difficult.' How should this be improved?

options.text: Replace it with objective behaviour and direct statements.
Ask another nurse to write it.

questions.rationale: Documentation should be factual rather than judgemental.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: When should medication administration be documented?

options.text: After the medicine has actually been administered.
At the end of the week.

questions.rationale: Records should reflect actual care and should not be completed in advance.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A nurse forgets to document an assessment completed earlier. What is the safest action?

options.text: Insert the note at the earlier time without explanation.
Ask a colleague to document it.
Make a clearly identified late entry according to policy.

questions.rationale: Late entries should be transparent and attributable.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which record best supports continuity of care?

options.text: A brief statement that the patient is stable.
Assessment findings, action taken, patient response and escalation.

questions.rationale: Records should show assessment, action, response and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A nurse posts a de-identified clinical story on social media, but colleagues can recognise the patient. What is the concern?

options.text: Confidentiality may still be breached through identifiable details.
There is no breach if the name is omitted.
Social media is acceptable after discharge.

questions.rationale: Removing a name does not guarantee anonymity.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A patient with capacity refuses a medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore concerns, confirm understanding, notify the appropriate clinician and document the refusal.

questions.rationale: A capable patient may refuse treatment, and the nurse should respond without coercion.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which action is outside the nurse's role when witnessing consent?

options.text: Confirming the identity and witnessing the signature.
Checking that the patient appears willing.
Providing a complex procedural explanation beyond competence or authority.

questions.rationale: Nurses should not provide explanations outside their role.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A patient lacks capacity for a particular decision. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the patient lacks capacity for all decisions.
Follow the local legal and organisational process for substitute decision-making.

questions.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific, and lawful processes must be followed.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which documentation practice is unacceptable?

options.text: Deleting or altering an entry to hide a mistake.
Correcting an error transparently according to policy.

questions.rationale: Deceptive alteration of records is unsafe and unprofessional.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A nurse receives confidential information unrelated to their patient's care. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Access the record out of curiosity.
Avoid access because there is no legitimate care purpose.
Save a copy for future reference.

questions.rationale: Information should be accessed only for legitimate care purposes.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A patient asks why information must be shared with another treating professional. What is the best explanation?

options.text: All staff may access any information.
Confidentiality does not apply in hospitals.
Relevant information is shared for legitimate care purposes to support safe treatment.

questions.rationale: Necessary care-related sharing should be limited and explained.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A student nurse asks to photograph a wound on a personal phone for learning. What should the supervising nurse do?

options.text: Allow it if the patient's face is excluded.
Ask the student to delete it later.
Decline and use approved organisational processes only.

questions.rationale: Personal devices create confidentiality and governance risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which entry is most objective?

options.text: 'Patient remained in bed and declined mobilisation after education was provided.'

questions.rationale: Objective records describe observable behaviour and actions.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: A nurse discovers that another person has entered information under the nurse's login. What should happen?

options.text: Ignore it if the information is accurate.
Report the security and documentation breach immediately.
Share the password more carefully next time.

questions.rationale: Records must be attributable and secure.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects lawful and professional documentation?

options.text: The record protects the nurse from criticism.
The record is timely, accurate, factual, attributable and shows care and response.

questions.rationale: These are the core characteristics identified in the notes.

questions.sectionLabel: Consent, Confidentiality and Documentation
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe consent and confidentiality practice?

options.text: Consent is informed and voluntary, refusals are respected and information is shared only with authority.

questions.rationale: Safe practice protects both patient choice and privacy.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A registered nurse delegates routine observations for a stable patient to a trained assistant. What must the nurse do?

options.text: Provide clear instructions, parameters and follow-up, then review the results.
Ask the assistant to interpret deterioration.

questions.rationale: Safe delegation requires direction, supervision and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which task should generally remain with the registered nurse?
questions.rationale: Assessment, clinical judgement, teaching and evaluation generally remain with the RN.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: An assistant reports that a patient's blood pressure has fallen significantly. What should the registered nurse do?

options.text: Ask the assistant to repeat it next hour.
Reassess the patient immediately and determine the required action.
Tell the assistant to call the doctor.

questions.rationale: The RN remains responsible for interpreting and responding to changes.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which factor should be considered before delegation?

options.text: Only whether the task saves time.
The task, patient condition, competence of the person, instructions and supervision needs.

questions.rationale: Safe delegation considers task, circumstance, person, direction and supervision.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A nurse disagrees with a colleague about a care plan. What is the most professional response?

options.text: Discuss the facts and patient needs respectfully and use the approved escalation pathway if unresolved.
Criticise the colleague in front of the patient.
Write a complaint before speaking with them.

questions.rationale: Professional conflict management is assertive, respectful and focused on patient safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which statement is assertive rather than aggressive?

options.text: 'I am concerned that this change may place the patient at risk. Can we review it now?'

questions.rationale: Assertive communication is clear, respectful and focused on the issue.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Hierarchy is preventing staff from questioning an unsafe order. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use respectful escalation based on facts and patient safety.
Ask the patient to challenge the order.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy should not prevent speaking up.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which situation represents unsafe delegation?

options.text: A stable patient's routine observations are delegated with clear parameters.
A complex assessment is delegated to an untrained assistant.

questions.rationale: Clinical assessment should not be delegated to an unqualified person.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: After a medication error, which reflective question is most useful?

options.text: 'What happened, why did it happen and what should change next time?'
'How can the event be kept private?'

questions.rationale: Reflection examines events, contributing factors and improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A nurse receives feedback that handovers are unclear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review examples, seek guidance and practise a structured handover approach.
Explain that colleagues should ask questions.

questions.rationale: Reflective practice uses feedback to improve future performance.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which outcome shows effective delegation?

options.text: The right person completes the right task safely, reports findings and the nurse evaluates the outcome.

questions.rationale: Completion alone is not enough; safety and evaluation are required.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A nurse asks an assistant to undertake a task without explaining when to report changes. What is missing?
questions.rationale: Delegation requires instructions and escalation parameters.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which approach is best when managing disagreement?

options.text: Focus on facts, standards and patient needs.
Seek support only after harm occurs.

questions.rationale: Professional conflict should remain evidence-based and respectful.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A nurse realises that stress affected communication during a shift. What is the best reflective action?

options.text: Ignore it because no complaint was made.
Review the event, identify triggers and plan a more effective response.

questions.rationale: Reflection supports learning, resilience and future improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A delegated task becomes more complex because the patient's condition changes. What should happen?

options.text: The task should be documented as complete.
The registered nurse should reassess and reconsider the delegation.
The assistant should independently change the plan.

questions.rationale: Delegation must be reconsidered when circumstances change.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which statement best describes accountability in delegation?

options.text: No one is accountable if the task was routine.
The nurse remains accountable for appropriate delegation and evaluation.

questions.rationale: Delegation transfers a task, not professional accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A colleague responds defensively when a safety concern is raised. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remain calm, restate the concern using facts and follow the pathway if unresolved.
Discuss the colleague's behaviour with patients.

questions.rationale: Assertive persistence protects safety while maintaining professionalism.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates reflective practice?

options.text: The nurse thinks about the shift privately.
The nurse identifies learning and changes future practice based on evidence and feedback.

questions.rationale: Reflection should lead to practical improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: A nurse delegates teaching about a new high-risk medicine to an assistant. Why is this unsafe?

options.text: Assistants may never speak with patients.
Teaching generally requires registered-nurse assessment, knowledge and evaluation.

questions.rationale: Teaching and evaluation usually remain with the RN.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Communication, Delegation and Reflection
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects professional communication, delegation and reflection?

options.text: Communication is respectful, delegation is appropriate and reflection leads to safer future practice.

questions.rationale: These capabilities together support safe professional nursing.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: An internationally qualified nurse is unsure whether a safeguarding concern must be reported directly to an external authority. What is the most professional action?

options.text: Consult local law, organisational policy and an appropriate senior clinician immediately.
Follow the reporting process used in the nurse's previous country.
Wait until definite proof is available.
Ask the family whether they want the concern reported.

questions.rationale: Mandatory-reporting duties vary between jurisdictions. Safe adaptation requires checking the local framework rather than relying on previous-country practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a professional code from a practice standard?

options.text: Codes are legally binding in every situation, while standards are optional.
Codes describe expected professional behaviour, while standards describe the level of practice required.

questions.rationale: Codes commonly describe conduct and values, while standards define expected professional performance.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: An IQN is asked to perform a procedure that was within scope in a previous country but is unfamiliar under the new employer's policy. What should happen first?

options.text: Proceed because previous registration confirms competence.
Ask the patient to consent to the uncertainty.
Verify local scope, policy and supervision requirements before performing the procedure.
Delegate the procedure to another new employee.

questions.rationale: Previous experience does not automatically establish authority in a new regulatory and organisational system.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which source most directly defines registration conditions and legal nursing authority?

options.text: The local nursing regulator and applicable nurse-practice law.

questions.rationale: Registration conditions and nurse-practice law define legal authority and obligations.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A workplace policy conflicts with the nurse's professional judgement about immediate patient safety. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Protect the patient, seek urgent clarification and escalate through approved channels.
Ask the patient to resolve the conflict.

questions.rationale: Policy supports practice but does not replace professional judgement or accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which situation may create a mandatory-reporting obligation, depending on local law?

options.text: Suspected abuse, serious misconduct or impaired practice.

questions.rationale: The notes identify suspected abuse, impaired practice, serious misconduct and communicable disease as possible reporting areas.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A nurse is unfamiliar with the local medication-checking process. What is the safest response?

options.text: Use the system from the previous workplace.
Complete orientation, review policy and request supervision until competent.
Ask another IQN to explain informally.

questions.rationale: Seeking clarification and supervised orientation are professional safety behaviours.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates personal accountability within an international team?

options.text: Assuming the team leader carries responsibility for all decisions.
Understanding local expectations and accepting responsibility for one's own decisions and omissions.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability remains personal even when care is delivered by a team.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A nurse discovers that a local code requires disclosure of a conflict of interest. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the local code and seek guidance if the process is unclear.
Use the previous country's rules instead.
Disclose only if a patient complains.

questions.rationale: IQNs must adapt to the local regulatory and professional framework.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which action is most appropriate when a legal requirement is unclear during urgent care?

options.text: Delay all care until a lawyer is available.
Provide necessary safe care within scope while seeking immediate senior or specialist advice.
Rely on memory from previous practice.
Ask the patient's relative to decide.

questions.rationale: The nurse should protect safety, remain within scope and obtain timely advice.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A nurse is told, 'This is how we always do it here,' but the practice appears inconsistent with professional standards. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the custom as local policy.
Copy the practice to fit in.
Check the applicable standard and raise the concern respectfully.
Document the concern only after harm occurs.

questions.rationale: Workplace custom does not override professional standards or legal duties.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates successful regulatory adaptation?

options.text: The nurse performs all tasks independently within the first week.
The nurse understands local laws, standards, scope and reporting duties and seeks advice appropriately.

questions.rationale: Safe adaptation combines knowledge, verified scope and appropriate consultation.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: An IQN notices a colleague showing signs of impairment while providing care. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Protect patients and follow local escalation and reporting requirements.

questions.rationale: Patient protection and local reporting processes take priority.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which statement about organisational policy is correct?

options.text: Policy provides local processes but must be interpreted alongside law, standards and patient needs.
Policy applies only to permanent employees.
Policy is optional for experienced nurses.

questions.rationale: Policies guide local practice but do not remove professional accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A new nurse has completed orientation but remains unsure about one high-risk task. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Perform it independently to build confidence.
Ask the patient whether supervision is necessary.
Request supervised practice and competency verification.

questions.rationale: Competence should be demonstrated, especially for unfamiliar or high-risk activities.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which professional behaviour most protects the public?

options.text: Relying on senior staff to notice problems.
Recognising limits, maintaining competence and reporting serious risks appropriately.

questions.rationale: Professional regulation is intended to maintain competence and protect the public.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A nurse learns that communicable-disease reporting differs locally. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review current local requirements and follow the designated pathway.
Use the process remembered from nursing school.
Share the diagnosis with all staff.

questions.rationale: Reporting requirements are jurisdiction-specific and must be verified.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: What is the best reason for an IQN to seek clarification?

options.text: It is a professional response when local systems, law or scope are uncertain.
It transfers accountability to the adviser.
It is required only during orientation.

questions.rationale: Seeking clarification supports safe practice and does not remove personal accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: A senior colleague instructs an IQN not to report a serious safety event. What should the IQN do?

options.text: Use the approved escalation or reporting pathway despite hierarchy.
Discuss the event outside the organisation.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy does not remove legal and professional reporting obligations.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe international professional practice?

options.text: The nurse adapts previous habits only when convenient.
The nurse relies on workplace tradition.
The nurse applies local law, standards, policy and professional judgement consistently.

questions.rationale: International practice requires deliberate adaptation to the local framework.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: An older patient with fluctuating delirium refuses a procedure. What is the nurse's best initial action?

options.text: Assess and support communication, seek timely clinical review and recognise that capacity may fluctuate.
Assume the patient lacks capacity because delirium is present.
Ask the family to consent immediately.
Proceed because the procedure is beneficial.

questions.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific and may fluctuate. It should not be removed solely because delirium is present.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which abilities are central to decision-making capacity?

options.text: Signing a form and agreeing with the clinician.
Understanding, retaining, weighing information and communicating a choice.

questions.rationale: These are the core functional elements described in the notes.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient understands information about a low-risk blood test but cannot understand a complex surgical decision. What principle applies?

options.text: The patient lacks capacity for all care.

questions.rationale: A person may have capacity for one decision and not another.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which action best supports decision-making before considering a substitute?

options.text: Ask the family to decide first.
Use simpler language, an interpreter, visual aids or additional time.

questions.rationale: People should receive practical support to decide wherever possible.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A family requests treatment that conflicts with the patient's clearly documented prior wishes. What should guide the decision?

options.text: The patient's known wishes, values, applicable law and best interests.
The opinion of the most senior relative.

questions.rationale: Substitute decisions should reflect the person's known values and lawful best-interest processes.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: What is the first step in a structured ethical decision framework?

options.text: Identify the ethical problem and gather relevant facts.

questions.rationale: A transparent process begins by defining the problem and facts.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which factor should be separated clearly during ethical reasoning?

options.text: Facts, stakeholder values, law, policy and professional obligations.

questions.rationale: Structured reasoning distinguishes these elements before options are considered.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient refuses a beneficial treatment for cultural reasons. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask family to override the refusal.
Assess understanding, explore the person's values and respect the decision if capacity and voluntariness are present.

questions.rationale: Autonomy applies to informed decisions that professionals may not prefer.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: When is ethics consultation most appropriate?

options.text: When complex or unresolved conflict remains after appropriate discussion and review.
When the nurse wants to transfer accountability.

questions.rationale: Senior, legal, ethics or specialist consultation may be needed when conflict remains unresolved.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient communicates a choice but cannot explain relevant risks or compare options. What should the nurse recognise?

options.text: Further assessment of understanding and weighing is required.
The choice must be accepted immediately.
The family should decide without assessment.

questions.rationale: Capacity requires more than expressing a preference.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which documentation best supports a complex capacity decision?

options.text: Information provided, supports used, the person's responses, consultation and reasoning.
A statement that the patient was confused.

questions.rationale: Transparent documentation should show the assessment and reasoning process.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient with fluctuating cognition is most alert in the morning. What should the team consider?

options.text: Making the decision at the person's best time where clinically possible.

questions.rationale: Timing may support the person's decision-making ability.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A substitute decision-maker requests an option that appears contrary to the patient's values. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Raise the concern and seek senior, legal or ethics review.

questions.rationale: Substitute authority must be exercised lawfully and consistently with the person's wishes and interests.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which statement about capacity is correct?

options.text: A diagnosis of dementia automatically removes capacity.
Capacity may fluctuate and should be assessed for the specific decision.
Only doctors may notice capacity concerns.

questions.rationale: Capacity cannot be assumed absent based on diagnosis or disagreement.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: An urgent intervention is required and the patient's decision-making capacity cannot be assessed fully. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delay all care regardless of risk.
Ask any family member to sign.
Follow the applicable emergency legal and clinical process and document the circumstances.
Use the process from the nurse's previous country.

questions.rationale: Urgent care must follow local emergency law and policy.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which approach best prevents coercion?

options.text: Presenting one option as the only responsible choice.
Providing balanced information and allowing voluntary choice.

questions.rationale: Voluntariness is an essential part of valid consent.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient needs an interpreter to understand a serious treatment decision. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange professional interpretation and reassess understanding.
Use a family member for convenience.

questions.rationale: Communication support is necessary for meaningful consent.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates supported decision-making?

options.text: The family makes the decision quickly.
The person participates as fully as possible using tailored communication and assistance.
The clinician selects the least risky option.

questions.rationale: Supported decision-making maximises the person's own participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: A disagreement between family and team remains unresolved after several meetings. What is the next appropriate step?

options.text: Seek senior review, legal advice, ethics consultation or specialist support.

questions.rationale: Unresolved complex conflict requires formal consultation.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects sound ethical decision-making?

options.text: Facts, values, law, policy and options are considered transparently and the reasoning is documented.

questions.rationale: A transparent, structured process is the defining feature.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: An IQN is asked to delegate a complex assessment to a worker whose local role excludes clinical judgement. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Decline, explain the scope concern and arrange an appropriate alternative assessment.
Delegate because the worker performed similar tasks overseas.
Ask the patient to accept the risk.
Delegate and review the result later.

questions.rationale: Titles and duties differ across systems; role boundaries must be verified locally.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which factor is most important before delegating care?

options.text: Patient stability, task complexity, local scope and the worker's competence.

questions.rationale: Safe delegation requires matching the task and circumstances to authorised competence.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: How should supervision be adjusted?

options.text: Use the same level for every worker.
Supervision ends after the task is assigned.
Match direction, monitoring and follow-up to patient risk and worker competence.

questions.rationale: Supervision should be proportionate to risk and capability.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A delegated worker reports a significant change in a patient's condition. What should the registered nurse do?

options.text: Ask the worker to decide the next step.
Wait for the next scheduled review.
Reassess promptly and determine the required escalation.

questions.rationale: Assessment, judgement and evaluation remain nursing responsibilities.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates advocacy?

options.text: Clarifying information and challenging an unsafe order respectfully.

questions.rationale: Advocacy may require respectful challenge to protect rights and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A patient from a minority group receives dismissive responses to repeated pain reports. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the pattern reflects different communication style.
Assess the pain objectively, advocate for equitable care and escalate if required.
Ask the patient to be more assertive.

questions.rationale: Advocacy includes challenging discriminatory or unsafe care.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which communication is most assertive?

options.text: 'I am concerned that the patient's condition is worsening. These are the changes, and I need urgent review.'

questions.rationale: Assertive communication is clear, factual, respectful and action-focused.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A colleague dismisses an IQN's safety concern because of hierarchy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discuss the colleague on social media.
Use structured communication and continue through the escalation pathway if unresolved.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy should not prevent escalation of safety concerns.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which task is least appropriate to delegate?

options.text: Routine observations for a stable patient.

questions.rationale: Clinical judgement generally remains with the registered nurse.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A worker accepts a delegated task but has not used the equipment before. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Allow the worker to learn during the task.
Provide training or reassign the task to a competent person.
Proceed if the worker signs responsibility.

questions.rationale: Competence must be established before delegation.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective supervision?

options.text: The worker receives clear direction, changes are reported and the nurse evaluates the outcome.

questions.rationale: Completion alone does not demonstrate safe supervision.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A patient needs help navigating several unfamiliar services. What is the nurse's advocacy role?

options.text: Ask the family to manage alone.
Clarify pathways, support communication and help coordinate access.

questions.rationale: Advocacy includes helping people navigate complex systems.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse disagrees with a medical plan but has incomplete information. What should happen first?

options.text: Clarify the facts and rationale before escalating the concern.
Tell the patient the plan is unsafe.

questions.rationale: Professional disagreement should begin with facts and structured communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: An assistant performs delegated observations but fails to report a concerning change. What should the registered nurse review?

options.text: The clarity of instructions, reporting parameters, supervision and competence.

questions.rationale: Delegation failures may reflect both individual and system factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which statement about delegation is correct?

options.text: Any task may be delegated if the ward is busy.
The nurse remains accountable for selecting, directing, supervising and evaluating delegated care.
Role titles are equivalent across countries.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability remains with the delegating nurse for the delegation process.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A patient's rights are threatened by an organisational process. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the process because it is policy.
Tell the patient nothing can be done.
Ignore the issue unless harm occurs.
Raise the concern through appropriate advocacy and escalation channels.

questions.rationale: Advocacy may require challenging systems that threaten rights.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which action best manages professional disagreement?

options.text: Structured communication using evidence and patient needs.

questions.rationale: Professional conflict should remain respectful and evidence-based.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether a local support-worker category may administer medication. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume equivalence with the previous country.
Verify the local role and policy before delegating.
Ask the worker what they usually do.

questions.rationale: Role titles and responsibilities differ across jurisdictions.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: A delegated task becomes inappropriate because the patient's condition becomes unstable. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the worker to make the decision.
Reassess the patient and revise or withdraw the delegation.
Document the change after the shift.

questions.rationale: Delegation must be reconsidered when circumstances change.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects interprofessional accountability?

options.text: The most senior clinician carries all accountability.
Roles are clear, concerns are communicated respectfully and unresolved risks are escalated.

questions.rationale: Accountability within teams requires role clarity and communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A patient with limited English is asked to sign consent using a relative as interpreter. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Pause and arrange a professional interpreter before the decision.
Proceed because the relative knows the patient.
Ask the relative to sign instead.
Provide a leaflet and obtain the signature.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation is required for complex or high-risk information when accuracy and confidentiality matter.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates cultural safety?

options.text: Using self-awareness, respectful enquiry and attention to how the patient experiences care.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety is determined through respectful, individualised care rather than assumptions.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A patient declines a care practice for cultural reasons that do not create safety concerns. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore and accommodate the preference where possible.
Ask family to persuade the patient.

questions.rationale: Cultural respect should be accommodated when clinically safe.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which situation requires a professional interpreter most clearly?

options.text: A complex consent or high-risk treatment discussion.

questions.rationale: Accuracy and confidentiality are critical in complex or high-risk discussions.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A family member answers every question for a capable patient. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Address the patient directly, explore preferences and ensure an opportunity for independent participation.
Ask the family to sign all forms.

questions.rationale: Power differences can limit participation; the nurse should support the patient's own voice.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which practice best protects digital confidentiality?

options.text: Using secure approved systems and sharing only necessary information.
Leaving records open for team access.

questions.rationale: Electronic communication requires secure access and appropriate sharing.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A nurse sends patient details to the wrong email address. What should happen?

options.text: Delete the sent message and do nothing else.
Ask the recipient to ignore it.
Follow the organisation's privacy-breach reporting and containment process immediately.
Wait to see whether harm occurs.

questions.rationale: Digital breaches require prompt containment and reporting.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which statement about family interpreters is correct?

options.text: They are always preferable because they know the patient.
They may interpret any legal discussion.
They remove the need to check understanding.
They may support the patient but should not replace qualified interpretation when accuracy or confidentiality matters.

questions.rationale: Professional interpreters provide accuracy, neutrality and confidentiality.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A patient says a care interaction felt culturally unsafe even though staff followed policy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Listen, reflect on power and communication, and explore how care could be improved.
Explain that policy proves the care was safe.
Ask the family to explain the culture.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety includes the patient's experience, not merely staff intention.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which handover feature makes responsibility clear?

options.text: A general statement that the patient is stable.
Structured information including current risks, actions, outstanding tasks and who is responsible.

questions.rationale: Structured handover should make risk and ownership visible.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: What is closed-loop communication?

options.text: The receiver repeats the message and the sender confirms it.
A handover completed by one person.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop communication verifies that a message was heard and understood correctly.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A verbal order is unclear during an emergency. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Read back the order and seek confirmation before acting.

questions.rationale: Read-back reduces misunderstanding in high-risk communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A patient requests that sensitive information not be shared with family. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respect confidentiality unless disclosure is legally required for safety.
Share it because family support is important.
Ask another clinician to disclose it.

questions.rationale: Patient preferences and privacy should be respected within legal limits.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which action best supports communication across cultures?

options.text: Checking understanding through teach-back and asking what matters to the patient.

questions.rationale: Understanding should be confirmed, and preferences should be explored directly.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A remote consultation takes place while other people can overhear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue because the patient joined voluntarily.
Check privacy and arrange a safer alternative if needed.

questions.rationale: Remote care requires active protection of privacy.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A patient's cultural preference conflicts with an immediate safety requirement. What is the best approach?

options.text: Follow the preference regardless of risk.
Explain the safety concern respectfully and seek the least intrusive acceptable alternative.

questions.rationale: Cultural respect does not remove safety responsibilities, but alternatives should be explored.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates culturally safe communication?

options.text: The patient can participate, understands information and feels respected rather than stereotyped.
The family agrees with the plan.
An interpreter is used for every interaction.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety focuses on the person's experience and meaningful participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: A handover omits who will follow up an abnormal result. What is the main risk?

options.text: Responsibility may be unclear and necessary action may be missed.

questions.rationale: Clear ownership is essential across teams.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which action best protects confidentiality during verbal communication?

options.text: Discussing patient details in a staff cafeteria.
Using initials in a public place.
Using an appropriate private setting and limiting information to those involved in care.

questions.rationale: Privacy depends on both audience and setting.

questions.sectionLabel: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects professional international communication?

options.text: The nurse uses one standard style for everyone.
Digital communication is used whenever convenient.
Communication is culturally safe, secure, structured and clear about responsibility.

questions.rationale: International professionalism integrates cultural safety, privacy and reliable team communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A nurse reports a medication error that was intercepted before reaching the patient. What is the most appropriate first response from the manager?

options.text: Confirm patient safety, thank the nurse for reporting and review individual and system factors before deciding a fair response.
Avoid documenting the event because no harm occurred.
Transfer the nurse to another unit.

questions.rationale: A just culture begins with safety, openness and fair review. Human error, at-risk behaviour and reckless behaviour require different responses.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which leadership behaviour most clearly demonstrates integrity?

options.text: Changing expectations according to staff seniority.
Applying standards consistently even when doing so is inconvenient.
Protecting the organisation's reputation by limiting disclosure.

questions.rationale: Integrity requires consistency between stated values and actual decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A senior clinician humiliates a junior nurse for raising a genuine safety concern. What should the nurse leader do?

options.text: Ignore the incident because the patient was not harmed.
Tell the junior nurse to become more resilient.
Address the behaviour promptly and reinforce that respectful speaking up is expected.

questions.rationale: Humiliation undermines psychological safety and may delay future escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects psychological safety?

options.text: Staff avoid errors because leaders are strict.
Only senior staff may challenge practice.
Staff can question, admit uncertainty and report concerns without fear of humiliation.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety supports open communication while accountability remains clear.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A leader says reporting is encouraged but repeatedly punishes staff who disclose near misses. What is the likely consequence?

options.text: Trust will weaken and staff may hide concerns.

questions.rationale: Inconsistent behaviour quickly weakens trust and safety culture.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which response is most appropriate for a one-time human error caused by a confusing electronic form?

options.text: Support, learning and redesign of the confusing process.
No review because the error was accidental.

questions.rationale: Human error calls for consolation, learning and system improvement rather than automatic punishment.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A nurse knowingly bypasses a safety control for convenience despite repeated coaching. Which just-culture category is most relevant?
questions.rationale: Repeatedly choosing a shortcut while underestimating risk is generally at-risk behaviour and requires coaching and removal of incentives for unsafe workarounds.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A staff member intentionally disregards a critical safety rule despite understanding the serious risk. What should leadership do?

options.text: Ignore the action if no harm occurred.
Treat the behaviour as ordinary human error.
Apply proportionate accountability while also reviewing system conditions.

questions.rationale: Reckless behaviour requires fair accountability, though system contributors should still be examined.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which leadership action best protects standards during workforce pressure?

options.text: Adjust workload and resources while maintaining core safety and ethical standards.
Ask staff to work faster without support.

questions.rationale: Ethical leaders place patient welfare above convenience or reputation.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A manager acknowledges uncertainty about a complex ethical issue and seeks consultation. What does this demonstrate?
questions.rationale: Ethical leaders explain decisions, acknowledge uncertainty and seek appropriate support.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates a strong ethical culture?

options.text: Staff speak up early, leaders respond fairly and standards remain consistent under pressure.

questions.rationale: A strong culture is visible in behaviour, reporting, fairness and reliability.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A leader publicly rewards productivity while privately asking staff to maintain compassionate care. What is the main risk?

options.text: Productivity has no effect on culture.
Private messages are stronger than public incentives.
The rewarded behaviour may dominate and compassion may decline.

questions.rationale: Leaders shape culture through what they reward, tolerate and address.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which mentoring approach best develops ethical reasoning?

options.text: Use case review, guided reflection and transparent reasoning about values, law and consequences.
Provide the correct answer without discussion.

questions.rationale: Ethical reasoning develops through structured reflection and explanation.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A leader receives repeated complaints that staff communication is coercive. What should happen first?

options.text: Defend staff because clinical outcomes are good.
Review patient experience, observe practice and identify system and behaviour factors.
Refer every complaint to legal services.

questions.rationale: Ethical quality includes dignity, communication and patient experience, not only clinical outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which action best models accountability after a leadership mistake?

options.text: Ask a subordinate to take responsibility.
Acknowledge the mistake, explain corrective action and monitor the outcome.

questions.rationale: Visible accountability strengthens trust and professional culture.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A service has a stated zero-tolerance policy for bullying, but senior staff are rarely challenged. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: Bullying is unavoidable in pressured settings.
Inconsistent enforcement is undermining trust and integrity.

questions.rationale: Standards must be applied consistently regardless of status.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which measure would best evaluate psychological safety?

options.text: Staff willingness to speak up, report errors and seek help, combined with response data.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety is reflected in staff behaviour and leadership response.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: A nurse who reported an error becomes isolated by colleagues. What is the most appropriate leadership action?

options.text: Address retaliation, support the nurse and reinforce reporting expectations.

questions.rationale: Retaliation threatens speaking up and should be addressed directly.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates ethical role modelling?

options.text: Leader decisions, communication and responses consistently reflect fairness, transparency and patient welfare.

questions.rationale: Role modelling is demonstrated through consistent action.

questions.sectionLabel: Ethical Leadership and Professional Culture
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 ethical leadership?

options.text: The nurse personally resolves every dilemma.
The nurse builds a culture where integrity, speaking up, learning and fair accountability are reliable.

questions.rationale: Global Nursing Professionals shape ethical systems, not only individual decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of professional governance?

options.text: To connect standards, competence, risk oversight and public protection.

questions.rationale: Professional governance makes accountability and standards visible across the organisation.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: An audit finds repeated incomplete consent documentation. What should the organisation do first?

options.text: Analyse the workflow and clarify where responsibility and understanding are breaking down.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins by defining the process failure rather than assuming individual negligence.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which credentialing practice is most reliable?

options.text: Verifying qualifications, scope and continuing competence before assigning responsibilities.

questions.rationale: Safe systems verify capability rather than assume it.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A nurse's formal qualification is current, but observed practice does not meet required standards. What should leaders do?

options.text: Continue practice because the qualification is valid.
Ignore the issue unless harm occurs.
Provide supervised remediation and reassess competence before independent practice.

questions.rationale: Credentialing and continuing competence are both necessary.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which data source may reveal a professional-practice improvement priority?

options.text: Consent audits, delegation incidents, privacy breaches and complaints.

questions.rationale: The notes specifically identify these governance indicators.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A policy is evidence-based but rarely followed. What should leaders examine?

options.text: Education, resources, workflow, leadership support and monitoring.

questions.rationale: Standards become effective only when implementation conditions support them.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates that a policy has changed practice?

options.text: Observed compliance and relevant patient or professional outcomes improve over time.
The policy is discussed at meetings.

questions.rationale: Implementation must be evaluated through actual practice and outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A committee identifies repeated delegation failures. What is the strongest first action?

options.text: Review role clarity, competence verification, instructions, supervision and follow-up.

questions.rationale: Delegation failures usually involve interacting governance and workflow factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which governance body has the broadest responsibility for organisational oversight and public protection?

options.text: Boards, committees, professional leaders and regulators working through defined structures.

questions.rationale: Governance structures distribute oversight across formal accountable bodies.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A professional complaint trend shows poor communication with patients from one language group. What should leaders do?

options.text: Analyse the inequity and redesign interpreter access, communication processes and monitoring.

questions.rationale: Data should be used to identify and address unequal practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which measure best tests documentation quality?

options.text: Timeliness, accuracy, objectivity, attribution and evidence of assessment, action and response.

questions.rationale: Quality depends on content and reliability, not volume.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: An organisation introduces annual competence checks but never follows up failures. What is the main weakness?

options.text: The governance process lacks action and accountability.

questions.rationale: Assessment must be linked to remediation, restriction or support where needed.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which statement best describes audit and feedback?

options.text: Audit identifies compliance, and feedback supports improvement and accountability.
Feedback is only for poor performers.
Audit is useful only after incidents.

questions.rationale: Audit and feedback help identify gaps and improve practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A serious privacy breach occurs because staff share passwords. What is the strongest governance response?

options.text: Remind staff not to share passwords.
Address access design, staffing workflow, education, monitoring and accountability.

questions.rationale: Strong responses combine system redesign and fair accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects effective credentialing?

options.text: Every staff member has a certificate.
Only appropriately qualified and competent staff perform defined roles.

questions.rationale: Credentialing protects patients by verifying authority and capability.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: A quality project improves documentation completion but patient understanding remains poor. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: Documentation and actual informed participation must both be addressed.

questions.rationale: The clinical example emphasises monitoring both documentation and understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
questions.stem: Which intervention best sustains professional improvement?

options.text: Embedding standards in workflow, resources, supervision, audit and feedback.

questions.rationale: Reliable change requires system integration and ongoing monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Governance, Regulation and Professional Quality Improvement
